title: Controlling a stage and managing product delivery
blurb: Follow a work package from the PM to the delivery team and back, and place each event in the right activity and workshop topic.
question: Pinewick Home and Garden's project manager chats informally with the product owner about risks, pulls figures from the team dashboard and updates the release map. Which activity is this, and how does it differ from evaluating stage status?

teach.h: The stage loop and the team loop
teach.body: Controlling a stage is the project manager's process: assign work, monitor it, handle issues, report progress to the board and take corrective action to stay within tolerances. Managing product delivery is the delivery team's side: it controls the link between the PM and the team by agreeing how specialist products will be accepted, built, reported on and delivered. In PRINCE2 Agile the link is a work package description made of a set of user stories, agreed between the PM and the product owner.

head: Activity
Agile flavour
rows: Co-create the WPD with the PO and team; confirm acceptance; review the team plan; update the release map
Informal talks with the PO; pull progress from the team dashboard; update the release map
Confirm the set of user stories or timebox features was delivered
Review stage progress in a progress review; update forecasts; confirm ownership transfers
Assemble team dashboards, project log and release map changes into the project dashboard
Log and manage them; seek board advice if needed
Check the deviation on the release map; recommend options in an exception report
Choose a fix and trigger it through a work package

What the delivery team does
rows: Reviews the stories; produces a team plan of what fits the constraints; reviews risks; agrees to deliver
Does the work; tells the PM about quality activities; gets approvals
Reviews registers and logs; updates the team dashboard for the PM to pull
Tells the PM the work package is complete

teach.h: Worked scenario: Pinewick Home and Garden's click and collect
teach.body: Patrick Dunne co-creates a set of user stories for live stock levels with Anita Shah, the e-commerce product owner, and her team. In their team planning workshop the team estimates effort and builds a team plan it can deliver in the sprint. The store operations team swaps its progress emails for a team dashboard, which Patrick pulls from. He feeds both into the project dashboard so the board, and internal audit, can see progress between stage boundaries. At the progress review, the team demos stock levels to store managers.

teach.text: Traps: 'evaluate work package status' is the PM's informal check with one PO and team dashboard; 'evaluate stage status' reviews the whole stage. The team plan is produced by the delivery team when it accepts a work package. The PM joins stand-ups only with the team's agreement. Forecast beyond tolerance means 'escalate issues and risks' with an exception report.

items: Work package = set of user stories agreed by the PM and the PO.
Team: accept (team plan), execute, evaluate (team dashboard), notify completion.
PM: authorize, evaluate WP status, receive, evaluate stage status, report highlights, issues, escalate, correct.
Team planning: backlog refinement, story refinement, effort estimation, iteration planning.
Retrospective: the good, the bad, the learning, team building. Progress review: highlights, risks, demo.

summary: You can now follow a work package between controlling a stage and managing product delivery and name each activity. You can also place discussions in the right topic of the team planning, team retrospective and progress review workshops, and use the right dashboard at each level.

A.q: Callowmere University's Student Support Hub is in stage 2. Project manager Jamal Hussain has an informal chat with Rebecca Lyle, the web team's product owner, about a new risk, collects progress from the web team's dashboard and updates the release map with actuals and forecasts. Which activity is Jamal carrying out?
A.why: Evaluating work package status means informal conversations with the PO, pulling progress from the updated team dashboard and updating the release map with actuals, forecasts and adjustments (Table 13.9).

whyNot.0: Evaluating stage status reviews progress for the whole stage, usually in a progress review, and confirms ownership transfers.
whyNot.2: Reporting highlights assembles dashboards and log changes into the project dashboard for the board.
whyNot.3: Receiving a completed work package confirms the set of user stories was delivered.

A.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's e-commerce team is in its team planning workshop for sprint 5. For each prioritized story, team members discuss how complex it is and how much work it involves until they share one view of the effort. Which topic is this?
A.why: Effort estimation estimates each prioritized story to reach a shared understanding of its complexity and effort (Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: User story refinement makes acceptance criteria clear and testable, agreeing what counts as done.
whyNot.1: Iteration planning comes after estimation and selects stories for the sprint to make a realistic team plan.
whyNot.3: Product backlog refinement clarifies and prioritizes requirements with MoSCoW.

A.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's software team is working on a set of user stories for the sensor dashboard. Near the end of the sprint it reviews its quality register and logs and updates its team dashboard so that project manager Andrea Lucas can pull current information. Which activity is this?
A.why: Evaluating a work package means the team reviews registers and logs and updates the team dashboard so the PM can pull up-to-date information (Table 13.12).

whyNot.1: Executing a work package is doing the work, telling the PM about quality activities and obtaining approvals.
whyNot.2: Notifying completion tells the PM the work package is complete.
whyNot.3: Accepting a work package reviews the stories, produces the team plan and agrees to deliver.

B.q: Easterholm County Council's digital team holds its team retrospective after sprint 6. A developer suggests pairing a social worker with a developer for each new form next sprint, to cut the rework seen this time. Under which topic should this suggestion be captured?
B.why: 'The learning' captures lessons and key takeaways and turns them into improvement suggestions and actionable insights for future iterations (Table 13.14).

whyNot.0: 'The bad' surfaces issues, risks and challenges and their causes; the improvement suggestion itself belongs to 'the learning'.
whyNot.1: 'The good' shares positives and celebrates wins.
whyNot.2: 'Team building' uses a game or food to strengthen bonds.

B.q: Larkspur Rail's Fair Fares project is in stage 2. At the progress review workshop, the app team shows members of the passenger panel the working one-tap delay claim and records their acceptance and comments. Which topic of the workshop is this?
B.why: The product demo shows completed features to showcase progress and gather user acceptance and feedback (Table 13.10).

whyNot.0: Project highlights reviews key metrics and achievements on the current project dashboard.
whyNot.1: Current risks and issues discusses and analyses what is open, not completed features.
whyNot.2: Wrap-up summarizes outcomes and agrees next steps.

B.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's project is in stage 3. Project manager Sally Greaves forecasts that two Must have stories for Release 2 cannot be finished by month 8, beyond the stage tolerance. She checks the release map for the size of the gap, weighs options against the canvas and recommends a way forward to the board. Which activity is this?
B.why: Escalating issues and risks examines the release map for the extent of deviation, assesses options against the canvas and release map, and recommends them to the board in an exception report (Table 13.9).

whyNot.1: Corrective action is taken by the PM within tolerance; a forecast beyond tolerance must be escalated.
whyNot.2: Capturing logs issues and risks; this goes further, to options and a recommendation for the board.
whyNot.3: Reporting highlights is the routine project dashboard update, not a recommendation on an exception.

C.q: Callowmere University's project is in stage 2. To keep a close eye on progress, project manager Jamal Hussain starts attending the web team's daily stand-ups every morning without asking the team. Is this an appropriate application of the 'controlling a stage' process, and why?
options: Yes, because the PM evaluates work package status in the stage
Yes, because the PM has direct authority over the product owner
No, because the PM should join stand-ups only with team agreement
No, because the PM should take progress from the project dashboard
C.why: The PM may attend daily stand-ups only with the delivery team's agreement; progress is pulled from the team dashboard (Table 12.1, Table 13.9).

whyNot.0: The PM does evaluate work package status, but through informal talks with the PO and the team dashboard, not by joining stand-ups uninvited.
whyNot.1: The PM does have authority over the PO, but that does not give the right to join the team's stand-ups without agreement.
whyNot.3: The PM pulls team progress from the team dashboard; the project dashboard is what the board pulls.

C.q: Pinewick Home and Garden's e-commerce team is about to accept a work package for sprint 6. To save time, project manager Patrick Dunne writes the team plan himself, listing every task and who will do it, and hands it to the team with the user stories. Is this an appropriate application of the 'managing product delivery' process, and why?
options: Yes, because the PM authorizes each work package for the team
Yes, because the PM has direct authority over the product owner
No, because the delivery team produces the team plan itself
No, because team plans are drawn up at the stage boundary
C.why: In 'accept a work package' the delivery team reviews the stories and produces a team plan showing what can be completed within the constraints; the PM reviews that plan when authorizing the work (Table 13.12, Table 13.9).

whyNot.0: The PM does authorize work packages in controlling a stage, but accepting the work and producing the team plan belong to the delivery team.
whyNot.1: The PM does have authority over the PO, but that gives no right to plan the team's tasks for it.
whyNot.3: The verdict is right but the reason is wrong: the team plan is made when the team accepts a work package in managing product delivery, not at a stage boundary.

C.q: Draycott Precision Engineering's board asks how it can see progress between stage boundaries. Project manager Andrea Lucas assembles the team dashboards, project log entries and release map changes and updates the project dashboard so board members can pull what they need. Is this an appropriate application of the 'controlling a stage' process, and why?
options: Yes, because report highlights updates the project dashboard
Yes, because the team dashboard replaces the highlight report
No, because this board is used to monthly written reports
No, because the project dashboard is kept for stage ends
C.why: In 'report highlights' the PM assembles team dashboards, the project log and release map changes and updates the project dashboard so the board can pull information (Table 13.9, Table 12.1).

whyNot.1: The team dashboard replaces the checkpoint report; the project dashboard replaces the highlight report.
whyNot.2: The board's habits are a tailoring concern, but they are no reason to say the dashboard approach is inappropriate.
whyNot.3: The project dashboard also replaces the highlight report and is updated regularly, not only at stage ends.

reteach.title: A restaurant kitchen on a busy night
reteach.question: How does the head chef hand out work, keep track of it and know when to tell the owner about a problem?

blocks.body: The head chef passes a ticket to a station. The station agrees what it can cook and plans its own steps, cooks, updates the board on the wall and calls 'ready'. The head chef glances at the wall board, chats to the station lead and, if the whole night is going wrong, tells the owner with options. After service the cooks talk about what went well, what went badly and what to change.

blocks.text: The head chef does not stand over the station uninvited. The PM joins stand-ups only with the team's agreement and pulls progress from the team dashboard.

explain.body: The PM co-creates and reviews the work package description with the PO and the delivery team, confirms they have accepted it and authorizes them to start. The PM reviews the team plan and updates the release map for the work authorized for the next iteration.

test.q: Larkspur Rail's project manager Rhys Pengelly co-creates a set of user stories for sprint 7 with Sasha Ellery and the app team, confirms they have accepted it, reviews their team plan and updates the release map. Which activity is Rhys carrying out?
test.why: Authorizing a work package is co-creating and reviewing the WPD with the PO and team, confirming acceptance, authorizing work, reviewing the team plan and updating the release map (Table 13.9).

whyNot.0: Evaluating work package status checks progress on work already under way.
whyNot.2: Receiving a completed work package confirms delivery at the end, not the start.
whyNot.3: Corrective action responds to a deviation; this is routine assignment of new work.

explain.body: When the work is done, the delivery team notifies the project manager that the work package is complete. Updating the team dashboard is part of evaluating the work package; telling the PM it is finished is a separate step.

test.q: Saltmarsh Housing Group's service design team has finished all the stories in its work package for the new call script. It now tells project manager Sally Greaves that the work package is complete. Which activity is this?
test.why: In 'notify work package completion' the delivery team tells the PM the work package is complete (Table 13.12).

whyNot.0: Evaluating a work package reviews registers and logs and updates the team dashboard.
whyNot.1: Executing is doing the work and obtaining approvals for completed products.
whyNot.2: Receiving a completed work package is the PM's activity in controlling a stage, not the team's.

explain.body: In the team planning workshop, iteration planning selects stories for the coming iteration based on priority and estimated effort, to finalize a realistic team plan that maximizes output and value.

test.q: Easterholm County Council's digital team has refined and estimated its top stories. It now chooses which stories to take into sprint 4, based on priority and the estimates, so that its team plan is realistic. Which topic of the team planning workshop is this?
test.why: Iteration planning selects stories for the next iteration by priority and estimated effort, to finalize a realistic team plan (Table 13.13).

whyNot.0: Effort estimation produces the estimates; choosing the sprint's stories comes next.
whyNot.2: Story refinement clarifies acceptance criteria so stories are testable.
whyNot.3: Backlog refinement clarifies and prioritizes requirements with MoSCoW.

explain.body: In the progress review workshop, 'project highlights' reviews key project metrics and accomplishments on the current project dashboard. Open risks and issues, and the product demo, are separate topics.

test.q: At Callowmere University's progress review workshop, the group walks through the project dashboard's burn-up chart, release status and key achievements since the last review. Which topic is this?
test.why: Project highlights reviews key metrics and accomplishments on the current project dashboard (Table 13.10).

whyNot.1: The product demo shows working features to users for acceptance and feedback.
whyNot.2: Current risks and issues discusses what is still open.
whyNot.3: The welcome sets out the agenda, goals and participants.
